name: Kerr's Black Hole in a Universe, and Kerr Radiating
description: Kerr's spinning black hole set radiating by Vaidya and Patel in 1973, its rotation parameter growing as its mass falls, and set by Vaidya in 1977 in Einstein's static universe and in an expanding universe with closed spatial sections. The radiating metric is a different one from the Kerr-Vaidya metric whose mass alone depends on the retarded time.
convention: We work in units with $c = G = 1$, so masses and times are lengths. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. Vaidya and Patel write the signature $(+,-,-,-)$, and each line element here is theirs with its sign changed.
history: Between July 1942 and April 1943, in Benares and under the guidance of Vishnu Vasudev Narlikar, Prahalad Chunilal Vaidya found an exact solution of Einstein's equations for the field of a radiating star [krasinski1999vaidya, vaidya1943]. Its mass drains away along outgoing null rays, carried off by the light the star pours out. To set that star spinning he studied the geometry of null curves in a rotating background, work that led him and his collaborator L. K. Patel to the radiating Kerr metric [krasinski1999vaidya]. Both signed it from Gujarat University in Ahmedabad [vaidya1973].¶Their solution of June 1973 is a field of flowing radiation with the symmetry of Kerr's spinning black hole, algebraically special and threaded by two geodesic null congruences free of shear [vaidya1973, kerr1963]. With one parameter set to zero it is static, and it is Kerr's metric. In the form Vaidya and Patel gave it in 1989, that parameter $a$ makes the square of the rotation parameter grow along the retarded time, $A^2 = k^2 + a\bar{u}$, while the mass falls as $1/A^3$ [vaidya1989kerr]. It is a different metric from the one often called Kerr-Vaidya, in which the mass alone depends on the retarded time and the rotation parameter stays fixed. For positive $a$ the mass and the angular momentum $mA$ fall together, and the Ricci tensor is that of pure radiation streaming outward along a single null direction. With the mass set to zero the spacetime is flat, however the rotation parameter runs.¶The coordinates come from a series of papers in which Vaidya built a frame for the general metric of Kerr and Schild [vaidya1977kerr]. Their time $t$ is the Galilean time of the flat background, the surfaces of constant $r$ are ellipsoids of revolution, and the retarded time $u = t - r$ stands in for $r$. In them Kerr's metric is flat space with a single term added, $2mr/(r^2 + a^2\cos^2\alpha)$ times the square of the null form $du + a\sin^2\alpha\,d\beta$, so Kerr's time is the time of the flat space beneath it [vaidya1977kerr].¶Vaidya's manuscript of 1 February 1977 puts Einstein's static universe of radius $R$ beneath that term [vaidya1977kerr, einstein1917]. He keeps the time, carries space over to rotating spheroidal coordinates, and writes $2m\mu$, with $\mu = R\sin(r/R)\cos(r/R)/M^2$, where Kerr's term has $2mr/(r^2 + a^2\cos^2\alpha)$. With $m = 0$ the field is Einstein's universe, and as $R \to \infty$ it is Kerr's black hole. The matter is a perfect fluid whose density and pressure the source shifts together, keeping $\rho + 3p$ at its value in Einstein's universe. Close to the black hole the density turns negative, and Dumitru Astefanesei and Eugen Radu, extending the nonrotating member maximally, found that the fluid the mass adds breaks the energy conditions in places [astefanesei1999]. At the antipode of the black hole, $r = \pi R$, that member holds a naked curvature singularity with no horizon around it [astefanesei1999].¶A factor $e^{2F(t)}$ across the whole turns Einstein's universe into a Robertson-Walker universe with closed spatial sections, and with $m$ scaled by $e^{-2F}$ in Kerr's term it sets the black hole in an expanding universe [vaidya1977kerr]. The cosmic fluid then carries one pressure along the direction $du + a\sin^2\alpha\,d\beta$ and another across it [vaidya1977kerr]. In the static universe the horizon sits at $R\tan(r/R) = m + \sqrt{m^2 - a^2}$, pulled in by a fraction near $r^2/3R^2$ by the curvature of space. In the expanding one the horizon exists while $a^2/m^2 < e^{-4F}$, and Vaidya concluded that early epochs of an expanding universe favour Kerr black holes far more than the present one does [vaidya1977kerr].¶In 1989 Vaidya and Patel joined the two threads in a radiating Kerr particle in Einstein's universe, its source a perfect fluid together with a stream of pure radiation [vaidya1989kerr]. The second solution of that paper fills a universe much like de Sitter's with pure radiation. Christian G. Böhmer and Peter A. Hogan, following the monograph on exact solutions, place the radiating Kerr metric of 1973 inside the complete axisymmetric family of such fields that E. Herlt found in 1980 [bohmer2017].

related.text: Kerr's black hole with the radiation switched off and the universe taken away. At $a = 0$ the radiating metric is Kerr's, and so is the black hole in Einstein's universe as $R \to \infty$ [vaidya1989kerr, vaidya1977kerr].
The universe the black hole sits in. With $m = 0$ Vaidya's metric is Einstein's static universe, written in rotating spheroidal coordinates [vaidya1977kerr].
The expanding universe around the black hole. With $m = 0$ the metric is a Robertson-Walker universe with closed spatial sections and its scale factor $e^{F}$ left free [vaidya1977kerr].
Vaidya's radiating star, the field that started it all. Here the star spins, and its rotation parameter grows as its mass radiates away [vaidya1989kerr].
Another mass in an expanding universe, this one round and still, held in a fluid at rest about it.
Kerr's black hole in a universe with a cosmological constant, the other way to put a spinning hole into a cosmos.

parameters.description: Mass of the black hole, a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Kerr's spin parameter, $a = J/(Mc)$, a length
Radius of Einstein's static universe
Vaidya's $M^2$, which is Kerr's $r^2 + a^2\cos^2\alpha$ as $R \to \infty$
Vaidya's $\mu$, which is Kerr's $r/(r^2 + a^2\cos^2\alpha)$ as $R \to \infty$
Zero on the horizons, and Kerr's $r^2 - 2mr + a^2$ as $R \to \infty$

coordinates.convention: Vaidya's coordinates with $u = t - r$ in place of $u$, then $dt \to dt - (2mR\sin(r/R)\cos(r/R)/\Delta)\,dr$ and $d\beta \to d\phi + (a/\Delta)\,dr$, which leave no cross term with $dr$, as Boyer and Lindquist's coordinates do for Kerr's metric. Vaidya locates the horizons in $t$ and $r$, where $\Delta = 0$.
